22455:
• Every classroom must be equipped with a sensor that continuously measures carbon dioxide in the air, within 6 months.
  • Maximum limit set at 1000 ppm of CO2, lowered to 800 ppm during a declared pandemic period.
  • The department must publish the sensor data on its website every week.
  • An action protocol must be applied by schools when the CO2 standard is exceeded.
  • Every classroom must have an air exchanger or purifier, supplied and paid for by the department, within 12 months.
  • Exchangers and purifiers must be inspected at least every six months, with reports made public.
  • The department must ensure annual follow-up on corrective measures taken as a result of inspections.

  • The committee must submit a report on the impact of the regulation, first in 2023 and then every 5 years

  • Removes the restriction limiting this right to the measures and standards provided for by law.
  • This change could facilitate legal recourse based on this environmental right.
22581:

22597:

22599:

  • Exceptions remain possible only where the Act itself provides for them.
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its official assent.
22639:

  • A report on gender- and diversity-based impacts must be tabled after each budget.
  • This report must also be tabled after an economic update announcing new measures.
  • The competent parliamentary committee must study these tabled reports.
  • The Minister of Finance will publish an annual analysis of the gender- and diversity-based impacts of fiscal measures.
  • The President of the Treasury Board will also publish a similar annual analysis of government spending.

  • The Minister becomes responsible for managing the national digital identity for everyone.
  • The Minister provides public bodies with services related to this digital identity.
  • A new national digital identity registry is created to store and share this data.
  • The Minister becomes the official source of digital data used for the digital identity.
  • The Minister must prepare an overall vision of telecommunications networks useful to the State.

25793:
• This bill strengthens secularism (separation between religion and state) in Québec's public and private schools.
  • It adds rules on religious symbols, uncovered faces, the conduct of students and staff, and the quality of teaching.
Part 1 Education Act
  • The public school system must respect democratic values, equality between men and women, and the secularism of the state.
  • Students must have their faces uncovered in schools, training centres, and during home schooling.
  • Parents of children in home schooling must also have their faces uncovered when receiving services from the school service centre.
  • Vocational training centres and adult education centres must also adopt codes of conduct.
  • The ban on wearing religious symbols now extends to more staff members of school service centres and to certain people under service contracts.
  • This new ban does not apply to staff already employed or contracts already underway when the law is passed.
  • The rules on staff requests for religious accommodation to be absent from work are clarified and tightened.
  • No religious accommodation is allowed when it would affect the duty to attend school, among other situations.
  • Decisions made by people who provide services to students, members of governing boards, and school service centres must be made without religious considerations.
  • The statements and behaviour of school service centre staff must respect the secularism of the state.
  • School service centres must adopt a code of ethics for members of governing boards.
  • School and centre premises can no longer be used for religious practices.
  • It is prohibited to influence, for religious reasons, the exercise of a power or duty set out in this law.
  • Teachers must submit a teaching plan to their principal, who must evaluate them each year.
  • A new committee on the quality of educational services helps principals monitor the quality of teaching.
  • The minister may set the exam schedule and order a school service centre to comply with a law or regulation.
  • Certain decisions by the minister, such as suspending or withdrawing a teaching licence, apply even if the teacher challenges them before the Administrative Tribunal of Québec.
  • More people working with students in a French-language school service centre must use only French.
Part 2 Education Act and Act respecting private education
  • Anyone providing services to students, or in contact with them, must have their face uncovered.
  • Students must respect equality between men and women and avoid any bullying related to racism, sexual orientation, gender identity, a disability, or a physical characteristic.
  • Schools must include these obligations in their codes of conduct.
  • Some of these rules apply even if they conflict with certain rights under the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms or the Canadian Constitution.
Part 3 Act respecting private education
  • Staff members of an institution not recognized for subsidies must also have their faces uncovered.
Part 4 Regulation respecting ethics and professional conduct standards
  • Technical adjustments to align this regulation with the new rules.

  • It also amends 20 other laws to adjust wording and powers related to constitutional matters.
Part 1 Constitution of Québec
  • States that its rules take precedence over any incompatible law, and defines the Québec nation.
  • Sets out the collective rights of the nation and the distinct values of Québec, including equality between women and men.
  • Includes human rights and freedoms and fundamental language rights.
  • Spells out the roles of the legislative, executive and judicial branches.
  • Sets out the principles guiding Québec in its relations with the outside world.
Part 2 Act respecting the constitutional autonomy of Québec
  • Provides for special sittings of the National Assembly to debate constitutional issues.
  • Bars certain bodies from using public funds to challenge laws that protect the Québec nation.
  • Requires the government to create a 10-year strategy on Québec's constitutional autonomy.
  • Allows the minister responsible for Canadian Relations to issue directives to departments on their dealings with Canada.
  • Allows the government to adopt a directive to prevent the federal government from encroaching on Québec's areas of responsibility.
  • Requires an owner to notify the minister before transferring land to a federal institution, in certain cases.
  • Spells out Québec's role in choosing senators and Supreme Court judges.
Part 3 Act respecting the Constitutional Council
  • Creates a new council that gives opinions on the Constitution of Québec or on federal initiatives, at the request of the government or the National Assembly.
  • Sets out how its members are appointed and for how long.
  • Allows the National Assembly's Office to adopt ethics rules for its members.
Part 4 Constitution Act, 1867
  • Removes the rules on the former Legislative Council of Québec, which no longer exists.
  • Replaces the word "legislature" with "Parliament of Québec."
  • Adds state secularism, the model of integration into the Québec nation, and the civil law tradition as fundamental characteristics of Québec.
Part 5 Civil Code of Québec
  • Specifies that the Civil Code applies in harmony with the new Constitution of Québec.
Part 6 Executive Power Act
  • Allows the premier to designate a person to hold the position of Officer of Québec (which replaces the lieutenant governor).
Part 7 Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
  • Specifies how to interpret rights and freedoms according to a balance specific to Québec with the collective rights of the nation.
  • In case of conflict, the right to equality between women and men prevails over freedom of religion.
Part 8 Code of Civil Procedure
  • Sets rules for requests to suspend the application of a law passed by the Parliament of Québec.
  • Prevents a court from raising a question about the constitutionality of a law on its own, or forcing the parties to do so.
Part 9 Wording changes across all laws
  • "lieutenant governor" becomes "Officer of Québec," and "Executive Council" becomes "Council of Ministers."
Part 10 Charter of the French Language, Act respecting State Secularism, and Act respecting integration into the Québec nation
  • Add the same declarations as the Act respecting the constitutional autonomy of Québec.
  • Several other laws (including the Courts of Justice Act, the Professional Code, the Act respecting Labour Standards, and the Securities Act) receive consequential adjustments linked to the new terms and the new Constitution.

26675:
• Brings in several measures from the March 25, 2025 budget, affecting pensions, vehicle registration, taxes and support payments.
  • Also amends dozens of municipal and tax laws for concordance adjustments.
Part 1 Act respecting the Québec Pension Plan
  • Work is considered to be performed in Québec, for the purpose of calculating pensions, only if it is carried out in Canada.
  • Months during which a person receives a reduced CNESST benefit no longer count in calculating their pension.
Part 2 Highway Safety Code
  • The vehicle value threshold triggering an additional fee rises from $40,000 to $62,500.
  • Electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles lose their exemption on the portion of their value between $40,000 and $75,000.
  • A new additional fee applies to electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles for their registration.
Part 3 Act respecting the Institut de la statistique du Québec
  • Sets out rules for when the Institute collects information for a public body.
  • Allows more researchers linked to a public body to use information held by the Institute.
Part 4 Code of Civil Procedure
  • Changes how the portion of a parent's income that can be seized for support payments is calculated.
  • Money received for an adult child can no longer be seized from the income of the parent who owes support.
Part 5 Act to facilitate the payment of support
  • A person receiving last-resort financial assistance no longer has to provide a guarantee to collect their support payments.
  • In a state of emergency, the Minister of Finance can adjust collection fees and advances paid to parents owed support.
Part 6 Tax Administration Act
  • Changes the definition of "large corporation" to account for the capital of related corporations.
  • Allows tax information to be shared with the Minister of Finance, without consent, to assess economic policies.
Part 7 Act respecting insurers
  • Life insurance companies will be able to obtain information about a deceased person, to inform beneficiaries of amounts owed to them.
Part 8 Act respecting municipal taxation
  • Municipalities will no longer be able to collect a business tax, except for certain fees from commercial development corporations.
  • Removes the option for municipalities to have an assessment roll based on rental value.
Part 9 Other measures
  • More money for the Fonds Avenir Mécénat Culture.
  • Revised fee for consulting the land register.
  • Higher government debt-reduction targets for 2032-2033 and 2037-2038.
  • The government will be able to change parental insurance plan contribution rates without a new vote in the National Assembly.
  • Several other municipal and tax laws receive technical concordance adjustments related to these changes.

  • Community pharmacies will no longer be free to use staffing agencies, except in cases allowed under a rule set by the Québec Cabinet.
  • A doctor who requires a payment from a patient will always have to give them a detailed bill.

26771:
• This bill merges, abolishes or reorganizes several public bodies to simplify government administration.
  • It also strengthens accountability rules for senior officials and reduces certain reporting requirements.
Part 1 Act respecting the Institut national d'excellence en santé et en services sociaux and Act respecting the Institut national de santé publique du Québec
  • These merge into a new body, the Institut québécois de santé et de services sociaux.
Part 2 Act respecting health and social services governance
  • Certain functions of the two merged institutes move to Santé Québec and the Minister of Health.
Part 3 Act respecting pre-hospital emergency services
  • Urgences-santé's board of directors will now have the same members as Santé Québec's board.
Part 4 Act respecting Héma-Québec and the Biovigilance Committee
  • Héma-Québec will take over the coordination of organ donations, which is being removed from Transplant Québec.
Part 5 Act respecting the Commission d'évaluation de l'enseignement collégial
  • This commission, which evaluates CEGEPs, is being eliminated.
Part 6 Act establishing the Office Québec-Monde pour la jeunesse
  • This body is being folded into the Ministère des Relations internationales et de la Francophonie.
Part 7 Act respecting the Office franco-québécois pour la jeunesse
  • Its internal structure is being revised.
Part 8 Act respecting the Centre de la francophonie des Amériques
  • This centre becomes a private non-profit organization instead of a public body.
Part 9 Act respecting the Ministère des Relations internationales
  • The Minister of the French Language gains new responsibilities over Canadian Francophonie affairs.
Part 10 Act respecting parental insurance
  • The Conseil de gestion de l'assurance parentale is abolished; Retraite Québec will now manage this plan and its fund.
Part 11 Act respecting the Ministère des Finances
  • The minister will have to present an overall financial plan to fight climate change in the budget speech.
Part 12 Act respecting sustainable development
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to decide, through a government rule, how to split surpluses from the Fonds d'électrification et de changements climatiques between the Generations Fund and the transportation fund.
Part 13 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale
  • This ministry's information technology fund is abolished, with its assets and debts moving to the government's general fund.
Part 14 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Enseignement supérieur
  • Fund 3 for university excellence and performance is abolished in the same way.
Part 15 Act to combat poverty and social exclusion
  • The Fonds d'aide à l'action communautaire autonome and the Fonds québécois d'initiatives sociales merge into a single fund.
Part 16 Public Service Act
  • The Commission de la fonction publique is abolished; its functions move to the Administrative Labour Tribunal.
Part 17 Act respecting administrative justice
  • The Administrative Tribunal of Québec will provide administrative services to the Financial Markets Administrative Tribunal.
Part 18 Act respecting the marketing of agricultural, food and fish products
  • The Régie des marchés agricoles will have fewer vice-chairs and fewer members to decide certain cases.
Part 19 Act respecting the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec
  • The Québec Cabinet will now appoint the SAAQ's vice-presidents and set their salaries.
Part 20 Act respecting the governance of state-owned enterprises
  • The management of Hydro-Québec, the Commission de la construction du Québec and other state-owned enterprises will have to be discussed before a parliamentary committee at least once every four years.
Part 21 Public Administration Act
  • Every state administrator will have to act with prudence, efficiency and fairness, and will go through a two-year probationary period.
  • During this probationary period, the Québec Cabinet can dismiss a state administrator who was not previously a permanent public servant, with only 15 days' written notice.
Part 22 Act respecting contracting by public bodies
  • Companies will no longer have to regularly renew their authorizations to contract with the government.
Part 23 Act respecting the Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales
  • This centre's contracts will now follow the same rules as those of government enterprises.
Part 24 Act respecting the Société d'habitation du Québec
  • Housing bureaus will be able to merge, and the government will be able to create them for any chosen territory.
  • Joint management of financial contributions by certain beneficiary organizations is ending.
Part 25 Several acts affecting the financial sector (securities, insurers, distribution of financial products)
  • Reduce the frequency of certain required reports and remove the obligation to produce certain documents.
Part 26 Act respecting the regulation of the financial sector

26993:
• This bill simplifies the operating rules of professional orders (such as the orders of nurses, pharmacists, agrologists, etc.) and allows certain health professionals to do more work.
  • It also changes the rules between pharmacists, manufacturers and pharmacy chains.
Part 1 Professional Code
  • Professional orders will be able to adopt certain regulations without the approval of the government or the Office des professions, which oversees them.
  • The Office des professions, which oversees professional orders, will now approve certain regulations instead of the government, such as codes of ethics.
  • Orders will be able to set, by simple decision, the conditions under which non-members may carry out certain activities.
  • The Office will now decide which diplomas give access to a professional permit, with the government's approval.
  • The Office must create a common rule for all orders to settle disagreements over professionals' bills.
  • The Office will be able to adopt regulations that apply to one or more orders at the same time.
  • The Office alone will set the ethics rules for members of the orders' boards of directors, and will be able to investigate and impose penalties.
  • Orders will have to add certain mandatory information to their public list of members (the roll), and will be able to add other information by decision.
  • The number of signatures needed to request a special general meeting of an order is changed.
  • People holding a psychotherapist permit obtained elsewhere in Canada under the Office's new rules will be able to practise in Québec.
Part 2 Act respecting nurses
  • Nurses will be able to order examinations and tests in more situations, not only in public health.
  • They will also be able to prescribe examinations, tests, medications, substances, products and dressings according to rules to be set later.
  • The rule that limited voting rights at general meetings to section delegates only is removed.
Part 3 Midwives Act
  • Midwives will be able to prescribe and administer contraception and screen for sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections in more cases.
  • They will also be able to treat these infections in a person without symptoms whose screening test is positive.
Part 4 Optometry Act
  • Optometrists will have fewer restrictions on the medications they can prescribe or administer, and on the care they can provide.
Part 5 Dietitians-nutritionists
  • Their scope of practice is updated, and they will no longer need a medical prescription to carry out certain reserved activities.
Part 6 Psychotherapy
  • The Interdisciplinary Advisory Council on the Practice of Psychotherapy ceases its activities.
  • Marriage and family therapists will be able to practise psychotherapy without a special permit, like psychologists and doctors.
  • The Office will be able to authorize people in training to carry out certain activities reserved for psychotherapists.
Part 7 Act respecting agrologists
  • The definition of practising the profession no longer requires that an act be done for payment to count.
Part 8 Pharmacy Act
  • The government will be able to allow a pharmacist to prescribe or substitute a medication with another made by a company in which the pharmacist has a financial interest, under specific conditions.
Part 9 Act respecting prescription drug insurance
  • A new rule will allow a drug manufacturer to pay certain benefits to an intermediary, such as a pharmacy chain.
Part 10 Regulation respecting drug manufacturers and wholesalers
  • Manufacturers will also be able to pay these benefits to drug wholesalers, not just to chains.
  • Various technical adjustments are made to several professional laws and regulations (the Bar, notaries, land surveyors, denturology, medical imaging technologists, legal aid, Charter of the French Language) to bring them in line with these changes.

27053:
• This bill amends several Acts to allow and regulate the exploration of underground reservoirs and certain fluids, and to allow a pilot project.
  • The bill does not allow activities already prohibited by the Act that put an end to hydrocarbon exploration and brine production.
Part 1 Act respecting the storage of natural gas and respecting natural gas and oil pipelines
  • A person must have a licence to explore or produce an underground reservoir or certain fluids below ground, except water.
  • The conditions for obtaining and keeping a licence will be set by a Québec Cabinet rule, without a new vote in the National Assembly.
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to set standards for work by regulation, including the authorizations needed from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy.
  • The Québec Cabinet will also be able to set rules by regulation for securing, closing, redeveloping and restoring sites.
  • Certain reservoirs or fluids belonging to the state may be reserved for the state or protected from any exploration or production, for example in an urbanized area or a protected area.
  • The minister will be able to temporarily suspend the granting of a licence on a piece of land while deciding whether to reserve it for the state.
  • A licence holder and a mining right holder on the same territory will have to agree on how they carry out their activities, according to rules to be set later.
  • The minister will have to monitor sites where carbon storage activities have taken place.
  • Documents sent to the minister by a licence holder will be public, except for exceptions set by regulation.
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to authorize the implementation of a pilot project for exploration or production.
  • Authorizations to build and use pipelines under the Act will now apply only to oil pipelines.

  • Conditions for carrying out work related to the new system must be included in municipal by-laws.

  • Persons with disabilities choose their own service providers and the terms of assistance.
  • Eligibility is conditional on residing in Québec, except for those living in a substitute living environment.
  • The benefit includes a base amount based on required hours, which may be increased for special needs.
  • Providers may perform actions that the person with disabilities would do themselves if not for their disability.
  • Provides for recourse through review before Retraite Québec, then before the Administrative Tribunal of Québec.
  • Retraite Québec must produce annual reports and an assessment after five years, tabled with the National Assembly.
27347:
• The bill amends the Flag and Emblems of Québec Act.
  • It officially recognizes the “Plaid du Québec” as the tartan of Québec.
  • This tartan is already registered in the Scottish Register of Tartans.
  • Its colours (blue, green, red, gold, white) reflect those of Québec's coat of arms.
  • The white recalls the scroll bearing the motto “Je me souviens.”
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its assent.
27349:
• Joint exercise of parental authority by both parents can no longer be automatically presumed to be in the child's best interest.
  • Custody granted to a parent found to be violent is presumed contrary to the child's best interest, unless proven otherwise.
  • That parent will have to prove sufficient guarantees for the safety of the other parent and the child.
  • Unproven allegations of family violence cannot be used against the parent who reports it or who is a victim.
  • Actions taken to protect oneself or the child are presumed not to be relevant in custody decisions.
  • These changes also apply to disputes over the exercise of parental authority, not only custody.

• Creates a Committee on Complementary and Integrative Health Approaches within INESSS.

• Limits the use of the Charter's notwithstanding clause to a serious and objective threat or the protection of French and Indigenous languages
  • Prohibits any override of the right to life and other fundamental rights protected under section 1
  • Requires a report from the Minister of Justice analyzing the impacts before any bill invoking the notwithstanding clause
  • Imposes a requirement for an advisory opinion from the Court of Appeal on the legality of the proposed override
  • Requires a general consultation in a parliamentary committee before the adoption of such a law
  • Requires the support of two-thirds of members, from at least two parties, to adopt an override
  • Limits the maximum duration of a provision overriding the Charter to five years
27655:
• Recognizes the right to food: physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
  • Requires the government to take measures to give effect to and protect this right to food.
  • Creates the National Committee on the Right to Food, made up of representatives from various sectors (community, Indigenous, school, health, agri-food, municipal).
  • The Committee advises the government, monitors the development of the right, and publishes a report at least every 3 years.
  • The government must assess the impact of its decisions on the right to food and mitigate any negative effects.
  • Aims in particular at access to adequate food at school and the reduction of food waste.
  • Amends the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms to include this new right to food.
27657:
• Recognizes the right of older persons to remain at home for as long as possible.
  • Guarantees access to affordable and adapted housing, and to financial security.
  • Protects against physical, psychological or financial abuse.
  • Entrusts the Commission des droits de la personne with monitoring compliance with these rights.
  • Creates a national strategy for the autonomy and home support of older persons.
  • Requires the government to publish a five-year action plan with concrete targets.
  • Provides for tax measures, rent regulation and support for caregivers.
27659:
• Reduces the base contribution rate for the Québec Pension Plan, which affects workers and employers.
  • Increases the small business deduction, which lowers the tax paid by these businesses.
  • Creates a temporary pause in Health Services Fund contributions for employers in agriculture, forestry and fishing.
  • Extends the tax credit for jobs in the Gaspé Peninsula and maritime regions, and expands it to seafood processing.
  • Expands the print media tax credit to news agencies and media that broadcast news bulletins on radio or television.
  • Extends the tax credit for the digital transformation of print media, but gradually reduces its rate.
  • Extends the measure allowing forest producers to spread their income over several years.
  • Eases the rules allowing certain films to qualify for cultural tax credits.
  • Adjusts the tax credits for e-business development companies that use artificial intelligence.
  • Changes the definition of "related individuals" for the transfer of used road vehicles, which affects the calculation of sales tax.
  • Also makes technical and consistency changes to several acts, with no new practical effect.

27679:
• The bill creates a new right allowing a person who is worried to obtain information about an intimate partner who may pose a risk to their safety.
  • It establishes a comprehensive process involving the Sûreté du Québec and a designated body to handle these requests and disclose the information.
  • New act respecting the disclosure of information: a person at risk, or someone acting on their behalf with their consent, may request information about their intimate partner.
  • New act: a minor aged 14 or over may submit such a request on their own.
  • New act: the government may, by regulation, designate other persons or categories of persons who may submit a request.
  • New act: police officers and workers from support organizations may inform a person at risk about the request process if it could benefit them.
  • New act: a police officer may, in these cases, disclose the identity of the partner who is the subject of a possible request.
  • New act: the Sûreté du Québec conducts the searches and transmits the relevant information to a body designated by the minister responsible for the status of women.
  • New act: a designated person, subject to regulatory conditions, meets with the person at risk to verbally communicate the information or the absence of relevant information.
  • New act: this person may also direct the person at risk to specialized resources and provide additional information.
  • New act: restrictions govern the disclosure to the intimate partner of the existence of a request and personal information concerning them.
  • New act: rules limit the further communication and use of the information obtained.
  • New act: certain persons benefit from immunity for acts performed in the exercise of their duties related to this process.
  • New act: these persons cannot be compelled to testify before a court concerning this information.
  • New act: penal offences are provided for breaches of the rules on communication or use of information.
  • Act respecting the Québec correctional system: revises the rules on disclosing to victims information concerning incarcerated persons or those under the supervision of correctional services.
  • Act respecting the Ministère de la Sécurité publique: consequential adjustments related to the creation of the new information disclosure regime.

27681:
• Proclaims November 5 as National Awareness Day for the issues faced by immunosuppressed persons.
  • Aims to inform the public about the increased risk of infections among immunosuppressed persons.
  • Recalls the symbol of the tilted red "i" adopted in 2023 to encourage social distancing.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
27683:
• Prohibits booking platforms from preventing hoteliers from freely setting their prices.
  • Also prevents platforms from limiting discounts or benefits offered by operators.
  • Any contractual clause contrary to this freedom is automatically considered invalid.
  • Applies to contracts between digital platforms and tourist accommodation operators.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
27695:
• Creates a mandatory "co-construction" process with First Nations and Inuit for laws and regulations that concern them.
  • Requires a preliminary analysis to determine whether a measure affects them, before initiating co-construction.
  • Requires contact with Indigenous organizations at least six months before a bill or regulation is introduced.
  • Creates a legislative reconciliation secretariat within the Ministère du Conseil exécutif to coordinate this process.
  • Provides for mediation or another mechanism if no consensus is reached between the parties.
  • Requires the government to review existing laws to make them consistent with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
  • Requires a government report on the implementation of the Act, tabled in the National Assembly every five years.
27705:
• Permanently fixes the electoral divisions of Gaspé and Bonaventure, despite the usual delimitation rules.
  • Increases the total number of electoral divisions in Québec to 126.
  • Also maintains the current boundaries of Matane-Matapédia-Mitis and Rimouski.
  • Requires the Commission de la représentation to publish a new list of electoral divisions.
  • Provides that this new list will come into force according to the end date of the 43rd legislature.
  • Creates a three-member committee to review the criteria for delimiting electoral divisions.
  • This committee must consult citizens and experts, and submit a report before February 1, 2028.
27715:
• Vocational training and adult general education must be offered in French.
  • This requirement applies to school service centres and subsidized private schools.
  • English remains permitted for persons already eligible for English instruction under the Charter of the French Language.
  • It becomes prohibited to allow a person to receive these services in English without being eligible to do so.
  • Penalties are provided for institutions that do not comply with this prohibition.
  • Persons already enrolled in English before June 30, 2028, will be able to complete their program in that language.
  • The Act will come into force on July 1, 2028.

27753:
• Creates a new position in the justice system, that of "special clerk," who exercises certain powers of a judge.
  • Sets out how these people are recruited, selected and appointed to this office.
  • Sets the length of special clerks' terms and the rules for renewing them.
  • Determines how their salary, benefits and other working conditions will be set.
  • Creates rules of conduct (ethics) that special clerks must follow, with a process for filing a complaint against them.
  • Specifies the tasks and powers that special clerks may exercise.
  • Creates a "coordinating special clerk" position responsible for overseeing the work of other special clerks.
  • Special clerks will be able to act anywhere in Québec, regardless of region.
  • Code of Civil Procedure: adjusted to recognize this new role in civil cases before the courts.
  • Courts of Justice Act: amended to incorporate this new office into the organization of the courts.
  • Act respecting the Ministère de la Justice: adjusted to provide administrative oversight of special clerks.
  • Youth Protection Act: technical adjustment to reflect the new position.

  • Creates two new government rules, with no further vote by the National Assembly: one on the recruitment of special clerks, another on their pay and working conditions.
  • Codes of ethics for lawyers and notaries, regulations on the selection of chairs of disciplinary councils and judges: consequential adjustments to align the rules with the new office.

• Allows a property owner to sign a voluntary contract to protect the biodiversity of their land.
  • The contract may be entered into with a municipality, an environmental non-profit organization, or an Indigenous nation or community.
  • The contract must be notarized and registered in the land register to be valid.
  • The obligations may last for up to 99 years.
  • The contract must precisely describe the monitoring and evaluation measures planned.
